intro: In the summer of 1787 a sickly Virginian sat at the front of a locked room and wrote down every argument. In the winter of 1962 a prisoner with a pencil wrote to the Supreme Court. Two hundred years apart, both men were doing the same thing: turning words about rights and power into something that would actually bind a government. This unit follows that work from the Enlightenment to your own county clerk's office.

The first chapter asks where the American design came from and how it works: the ideas the founders borrowed, the failed first government, the compromises of Philadelphia, the fight to ratify, and the machinery of federalism, separated powers, and checks that still runs today, in Washington and in Springfield. The second chapter asks what the design gives a person: liberties that fence in the government, rights to equal treatment, the landmark cases that made those words enforceable, and the elections, groups, polls, and meetings through which ordinary people push back.

By the end you should be able to explain how a bill becomes law and how a court can undo it, why a right can sit unused in the text for eighty years, what the Electoral College does and why people argue about it, how to read a poll, and exactly what you would do, this month, to change a decision in your town. Civics is not a subject about other people. It is the owner's manual for the power you already hold.
bigQuestion: Where does government power come from, how is it limited, and what can one person do to shape it?

timeline.t: John Locke publishes his argument that governments exist to protect natural rights
The Stamp Act sparks the colonial claim of no taxation without representation
The Declaration of Independence states the theory of consent and lists the evidence
The Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia; Madison keeps the only full record
The Bill of Rights is ratified as the price of the Federalists' victory
Marbury v. Madison establishes judicial review
The Fourteenth Amendment promises due process and equal protection from the states
Brown v. Board of Education declares segregated schools inherently unequal
Gideon v. Wainwright guarantees poor defendants a lawyer
Illinois voters approve the state's fourth and current constitution
The Supreme Court orders Nixon to hand over the tapes; he resigns within weeks
McDonald v. Chicago applies the Second Amendment to states and cities

words.d: the idea that people agree to be governed in exchange for protection of their rights
agreement; the principle that government may act only with the approval of the governed
the 1787 deal giving states equal Senate votes and population-based House seats
to formally approve a constitution or amendment
a system dividing power between a national government and state governments
the powers each branch has to limit or block the other branches
the power of courts to strike down laws that violate the Constitution
freedoms the government may not take away, such as speech and religion
the Fourteenth Amendment rule that government must treat people equally under the law
applying rights in the Bill of Rights to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment
the 538 electors, chosen by the states, who formally elect the president
the range within which a poll's result is likely to differ from the true value

test.q: Which idea did Thomas Jefferson borrow from John Locke for the Declaration of Independence?
choices: Governments exist to protect natural rights and rest on consent
Power should be split among three branches
Kings rule by God's choice
Large republics are safer than small ones
test.why: Jefferson rewrote Locke's argument that people have natural rights and that governments derive their power from the governed.

test.q: What was the most serious weakness of the Articles of Confederation?
choices: The president had too much power
Congress could not tax or enforce its decisions
The states had no legislatures
It required a bill of rights
test.why: Congress could only ask states for money and had no way to pay debts or respond to Shays's Rebellion.

test.q: Why does every state have two senators regardless of population?
choices: Because the Articles required it
Because of the Three-Fifths Compromise
Because of the Great Compromise between large and small states
Because the Senate was added by amendment
test.why: The Great Compromise gave small states equal Senate votes while the House follows population.

test.q: What was Madison's argument in Federalist Number 51?
choices: The Constitution needed no changes
The states should keep all power
Rights should be listed in the text
A government must control the governed and also control itself
test.why: Madison argued that because people are not angels, government needs both power and internal checks.

test.q: An amendment is proposed by two thirds of Congress. What must happen next?
choices: Three fourths of the states must ratify it
The president must sign it
The Supreme Court must approve it
A majority of voters must approve it
test.why: Article Five requires ratification by three fourths of the states, thirty-eight of fifty today.

test.q: Which is an example of a concurrent power?
choices: Declaring war
Taxing
Coining money
Running the post office
test.why: Both national and state governments tax; the other powers are enumerated for the national government alone.

test.q: The president vetoes a bill. What can Congress do?
choices: Nothing; the veto is final
Ask the Supreme Court to overturn the veto
Override it with a two-thirds vote in each house
Impeach the president automatically
test.why: A two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate overrides a veto and makes the bill law.

test.q: How does the Illinois Constitution differ from the U.S. Constitution in amending?
choices: Illinois never allows amendments
Illinois requires all counties to agree
Illinois amendments need the governor's signature
Illinois voters approve amendments directly at an election
test.why: After a three-fifths vote of the General Assembly, Illinois amendments go to the voters; federal amendments go to state legislatures or conventions.

test.q: A city refuses to grant a marching permit to one ethnic group but grants it to all others. Which protection is at stake?
choices: Equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment
The establishment clause
The right to bear arms
Due process in a criminal trial
test.why: Unequal treatment based on who people are is a civil rights problem governed by equal protection.

test.q: Why does the Fourth Amendment protect you from a state police officer today when it did not in 1833?
choices: The amendment was rewritten in 1961
The Supreme Court incorporated it through the Fourteenth Amendment
States adopted the Bill of Rights by vote
Congress passed a law applying it to states
test.why: Incorporation, decided case by case, applied the Fourth Amendment to state police in 1961.

test.q: What did McCulloch against Maryland decide about national power?
choices: Congress may exercise only listed powers
States may tax federal agencies
Congress has implied powers to carry out its listed ones, and states cannot tax federal institutions
The Supreme Court cannot review state laws
test.why: Marshall read the necessary and proper clause broadly and held that the power to tax involves the power to destroy.

test.q: Under Tinker, a school may limit student speech only when it
choices: is political
criticizes a teacher
happens during class
would substantially disrupt school work or invade others' rights
test.why: The Court protected silent armbands and set substantial disruption as the test for limiting student speech.

test.q: What was the flaw in the 1936 Literary Digest poll?
choices: Its sample was large but not random
It asked too few people
It polled only Democrats
It was taken after the election
test.why: Lists of car and phone owners skewed wealthy, so millions of responses still misrepresented the electorate.

test.q: In Illinois, when may a seventeen-year-old vote?
choices: Never; the age is eighteen
In a primary, if the voter will be eighteen by the general election
In any election with parental permission
Only in school board elections
test.why: Illinois lets seventeen-year-olds who will be eighteen by the general election vote in the primary.

test.q: Which action best matches what the unit calls organizing?
choices: Posting an opinion online
Voting in a primary
Gathering neighbors around a specific demand and dividing the work
Reading a poll carefully
test.why: Organizing brings people who share a concern together around a demand and a plan, turning one voice into power.

write.prompt: Take a position: Does the American system of checks, courts, and elections give an ordinary person real power over government, or only the appearance of it? Support your claim with evidence from at least two cases or events in this unit and address the strongest argument on the other side.
tips: State your claim in one sentence, choosing real power or the appearance of it, and stick to it.
Use specific evidence: Gideon's pencil letter, the Nixon tapes, the Anti-Federalists winning the Bill of Rights, the Literary Digest failure, or turnout by age.
Explain your reasoning: show how each piece of evidence connects to your claim rather than just listing it.
Address the other side honestly: money in politics, low turnout, or the slowness of the amendment process, and explain why your claim still holds.
End by saying what one person could actually do this year, based on the tools in chapter 44.
